```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(scales)
library(ggrepel)

# Consistent colours
orange <- "#E8672C"
blue   <- "#1769AA"
green  <- "#2D8C63"
grey   <- "#C7CED4"

# Check that the files exist
price_file <- "data/City_metrics_public_10-2026.xlsx"
index_file <- "data/City_Metrics_rents_sales-Mietpreis-Transaktionspreisindex.xlsx"
e8_file    <- "data/E8_topic_E__Housing_situation.xlsx"

stopifnot(file.exists(price_file))
stopifnot(file.exists(index_file))
stopifnot(file.exists(e8_file))

# Read the datasets
rent_prices <- read_excel(price_file)
rent_index  <- read_excel(index_file)
e8_housing  <- read_excel(
  e8_file,
  sheet = "housing_form_aggregated_all",
  skip = 3
)

selected_cities <- c(
  "Berlin", "Bonn", "Bremen", "Dresden",
  "Frankfurt am Main", "Hamburg", "Köln",
  "Leipzig", "München", "Münster"
)

# Use complete annual, nominal observations only
annual_rents <- rent_prices |>
  filter(
    City %in% selected_cities,
    is.na(Quarter),
    is.na(Month),
    Inflation_adjusted == 0,
    Year >= 2015,
    Year <= 2025
  )
```

## A university choice is also a housing choice

A student choosing where to study does not enter one German rental market.

The student enters a **specific city market**, with its own rent level and rate of change.

::: {.fragment}
### The same housing budget can provide very different options across university cities.
:::

::: notes
This is the setting of the story. Students study within the same national higher-education system, but local rental conditions differ strongly.
:::

## The question behind our story

### How is student housing pressure changing across selected German university cities?

We follow three questions:

1. How large is the current asking-rent gap?
2. Which lower-cost cities are becoming expensive quickly?
3. How many students have access to dedicated student accommodation?

::: notes
We use the term housing pressure because complete affordability requires city-level student income and total housing-cost data, which are not available in these datasets.
:::

## Two datasets reveal two sides of the problem

::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
### GREIX

- Median asking rent per square metre
- City-level rent growth
- Nominal and inflation-adjusted indices
- Main comparison: 2015 to 2025
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### EUROSTUDENT 8

- Student housing arrangements
- Living with parents
- Dedicated student accommodation
- Living alone or with others
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note}
GREIX describes local rental markets. EUROSTUDENT provides the student-specific context. The datasets are interpreted together, but they are not merged row by row.
:::

## Method: level, change and exposure

::: columns
::: {.column width="32%"}
### Current level
Median asking rent in 2025
:::

::: {.column width="32%"}
### Change
Percentage growth from 2015 to 2025
:::

::: {.column width="32%"}
### Student exposure
Housing arrangements in Germany
:::
:::

We use annual observations and keep nominal and inflation-adjusted values separate.

## The first warning sign is a large city gap

```{r}
#| label: fig-current-rents
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5.3
#| out-width: "95%"

rent_2025 <- annual_rents |>
  filter(Year == 2025) |>
  arrange(MED_PRICE_SQM) |>
  mutate(
    highlight = case_when(
      City == "München" ~ "Highest",
      City == "Dresden" ~ "Lowest",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  )

rent_gap <- max(rent_2025$MED_PRICE_SQM, na.rm = TRUE) -
  min(rent_2025$MED_PRICE_SQM, na.rm = TRUE)

ggplot(rent_2025,
       aes(x = reorder(City, MED_PRICE_SQM),
           y = MED_PRICE_SQM,
           fill = highlight)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0("€", number(MED_PRICE_SQM, accuracy = 0.01))),
    hjust = -0.12,
    size = 4
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Highest" = orange,
    "Lowest" = green,
    "Other" = grey
  )) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 25),
    breaks = seq(0, 25, 5),
    labels = label_number(prefix = "€")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = paste0("A €", number(rent_gap, accuracy = 0.01),
                   " gap separates the highest and lowest city"),
    subtitle = "Median asking rent per square metre, 2025",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Median asking rent per m²",
    caption = "Source: GREIX. Annual nominal asking rents."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

::: notes
München has the highest median asking rent in the selected sample, while Dresden has the lowest. The gap establishes the unequal local markets students enter.
:::

## The same small apartment can imply a very different monthly rent

```{r}
#| label: monthly-example
#| include: false
munich_rate <- rent_2025 |> filter(City == "München") |> pull(MED_PRICE_SQM)
dresden_rate <- rent_2025 |> filter(City == "Dresden") |> pull(MED_PRICE_SQM)
munich_30 <- munich_rate * 30
dresden_30 <- dresden_rate * 30
monthly_gap <- munich_30 - dresden_30
```

::: columns
::: {.column width="47%"}
### München

# `r paste0("€", scales::number(munich_30, accuracy = 1))`

Illustrative monthly base asking rent for 30 m²
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
### Dresden

# `r paste0("€", scales::number(dresden_30, accuracy = 1))`

Illustrative monthly base asking rent for 30 m²
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
The illustrative monthly difference is approximately **`r paste0("€", scales::number(monthly_gap, accuracy = 1))`** before utilities and other costs.
:::

## But the current price is only half the story

A lower-cost city may appear affordable today while moving quickly towards a higher-cost market.

### Which cities experienced the fastest rent growth?

## Some lower-cost cities are catching up quickly

```{r}
#| label: fig-growth
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5.3
#| out-width: "95%"

growth_data <- annual_rents |>
  filter(Year %in% c(2015, 2025)) |>
  select(City, Year, MED_PRICE_SQM) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = Year,
    values_from = MED_PRICE_SQM,
    names_prefix = "rent_"
  ) |>
  drop_na(rent_2015, rent_2025) |>
  mutate(
    growth = 100 * (rent_2025 - rent_2015) / rent_2015,
    highlight = case_when(
      City == "Berlin" ~ "Fastest",
      City == "Leipzig" ~ "Lower-cost growth",
      City == "Dresden" ~ "Slower growth",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(growth)

ggplot(growth_data,
       aes(x = reorder(City, growth),
           y = growth,
           fill = highlight)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(growth), "%")),
    hjust = -0.15,
    size = 4
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Fastest" = orange,
    "Lower-cost growth" = "#F4A261",
    "Slower growth" = green,
    "Other" = grey
  )) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, max(growth_data$growth) * 1.15),
    labels = label_percent(scale = 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Lower-cost did not always mean slow-growing",
    subtitle = "Change in median asking rent, 2015 to 2025",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Growth",
    caption = "Source: GREIX. Annual nominal asking rents."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

::: notes
Berlin recorded the fastest growth. Leipzig matters because it began as a lower-cost city but experienced strong growth. Dresden shows that the pattern is not uniform.
:::

## The affordability map is shifting, but not uniformly

```{r}
#| label: fig-relationship
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| out-width: "92%"

median_start <- median(growth_data$rent_2015, na.rm = TRUE)
median_growth <- median(growth_data$growth, na.rm = TRUE)

relationship_data <- growth_data |>
  mutate(
    group = case_when(
      rent_2015 < median_start & growth > median_growth ~
        "Lower start, faster growth",
      City == "Dresden" ~
        "Lower start, slower growth",
      TRUE ~ "Other cities"
    )
  )

ggplot(relationship_data,
       aes(x = rent_2015,
           y = growth,
           label = City,
           colour = group)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median_start,
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = median_growth,
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 4.5) +
  geom_text_repel(size = 4, box.padding = 0.5,
                  max.overlaps = Inf, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Lower start, faster growth" = orange,
    "Lower start, slower growth" = green,
    "Other cities" = blue
  )) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(prefix = "€")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Previously cheaper cities followed different paths",
    subtitle = "Starting asking rent in 2015 compared with growth to 2025",
    x = "Median asking rent in 2015 per m²",
    y = "Growth from 2015 to 2025",
    colour = NULL,
    caption = "Source: GREIX."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

::: notes
Leipzig and Bremen combine lower starting rents with faster growth. Dresden began at a lower rent but followed a slower-growth path. Affordable alternatives are shifting rather than disappearing everywhere at the same rate.
:::

## Rental growth cannot be explained by general inflation alone

```{r}
#| label: fig-inflation
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 5.3
#| out-width: "92%"

# Accept either spelling of the GREIX aggregate
inflation_data <- rent_index |>
  filter(
    str_to_lower(City) == "greix",
    !is.na(Quarter)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    time = Year + (Quarter - 1) / 4,
    type = if_else(
      Inflation_adjusted == 1,
      "Inflation-adjusted index",
      "Nominal index"
    )
  )

ggplot(inflation_data,
       aes(x = time, y = Rent_Index, colour = type)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Nominal index" = orange,
    "Inflation-adjusted index" = blue
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "Part of the rent increase remains after inflation",
    subtitle = "GREIX quarterly rent index",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Rent index",
    colour = NULL,
    caption = "Source: GREIX rental and transaction price index."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

::: notes
The nominal line shows rent growth before inflation is removed. The inflation-adjusted line shows the remaining change. A rising real index indicates that rents increased faster than the general price level.
:::

## The climax: rising rents meet limited student housing

The rental-market evidence creates the pressure.

The student-housing evidence shows why the pressure matters.

### How many students live in dedicated student accommodation?

## Dedicated student accommodation reaches only a minority

```{r}
#| label: fig-student-housing
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 5.3
#| out-width: "92%"

student_housing <- e8_housing |>
  filter(
    FG == "all_students",
    FGI == "all",
    I == "accom_aggregated"
  ) |>
  transmute(
    indicator = as.character(II),
    percentage = as.numeric(DE)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    housing_type = case_when(
      indicator == "1" ~ "With parents",
      indicator == "2" ~ "Student accommodation",
      indicator == "3" ~ "With partner or children",
      indicator == "4" ~ "With other people",
      indicator == "5" ~ "Living alone",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(housing_type))

# Convert proportions to percentages only when necessary
if (max(student_housing$percentage, na.rm = TRUE) <= 1) {
  student_housing <- student_housing |>
    mutate(percentage = percentage * 100)
}

student_housing <- student_housing |>
  mutate(
    highlight = if_else(
      housing_type == "Student accommodation",
      "Student accommodation",
      "Other arrangement"
    )
  )

ggplot(student_housing,
       aes(x = reorder(housing_type, percentage),
           y = percentage,
           fill = highlight)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(number(percentage, accuracy = 0.1), "%")),
    hjust = -0.12,
    size = 4
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Student accommodation" = orange,
    "Other arrangement" = grey
  )) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, max(student_housing$percentage) * 1.2),
    labels = label_percent(scale = 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Dedicated student housing reaches only a minority",
    subtitle = "Housing arrangements of students in Germany",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Students",
    caption = "Source: EUROSTUDENT 8, Topic E."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

::: notes
Dedicated student accommodation houses only a minority of students. Students outside student accommodation are not automatically private renters because some live with parents or partners. The point is that student-specific accommodation has limited reach.
:::

## Two pressures now meet

::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Local market pressure

- Large rental gaps between cities
- Rapid growth in some cheaper markets
- Increases partly remain after inflation
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
### Limited student-specific coverage

- Dedicated accommodation reaches a minority
- Many students use other arrangements
- Exposure differs across student groups
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
Students face unequal and changing local rental markets while dedicated student accommodation has limited reach.
:::

## What the evidence means

1. **Location matters:** the same budget provides different housing options.
2. **Timing matters:** a lower-cost city can become expensive quickly.
3. **Housing type matters:** dedicated accommodation can reduce exposure to the wider market.
4. **The pattern is uneven:** Leipzig and Bremen show pressure, while Dresden remains an important exception.

## What the evidence cannot yet tell us

- Student income by city
- The share of income spent on rent
- Final contracted rent
- Utilities and total housing expenses
- Student-residence prices by city
- Why students choose specific housing arrangements

::: {.callout-note}
The project measures **student housing pressure**, not a complete city-level affordability ratio.
:::

## The map of lower-cost university cities is shifting

::: {.callout-tip}
### Main insight

**Students enter sharply different private rental markets, and rapid rent growth in some previously cheaper cities means that lower-cost alternatives are becoming less secure.**
:::

Dedicated student accommodation reaches only a minority, making wider rental-market conditions important to the student housing story.

## A better response requires better local evidence

- Expand dedicated student accommodation where rent growth and student demand are both high.
- Publish city-level student rent and income indicators.
- Monitor formerly cheaper university cities before affordability declines further.
- Keep student housing policy connected to wider rental-market policy.
